blocks.body: The down payment is a near-term goal saved in safe assets, and closing costs come on top of it; the emergency fund is a different pool and should still be whole after closing, because new owners take on repairs a landlord used to pay for. A pre-approval is the most a lender will lend, not a budget, so price the full monthly cost, including property taxes, insurance, any HOA fees and upkeep. HUD-approved housing counselors advise at little or no cost and can point you to down-payment help. Avoid applying for a lot of new credit while you prepare for the mortgage.
blocks.plain: Your down payment is a short-term goal kept in safe places, and you also need money for closing costs. Your emergency fund is separate money, and it should still be full after closing. As an owner, you now pay for repairs a landlord used to cover. A pre-approval shows the most a lender will lend you. It is not your budget. Add up the full monthly cost: property taxes, insurance, any HOA fees, and upkeep. HUD-approved housing counselors give advice for little or no cost and can help you find down-payment help. Try not to apply for a lot of new credit while you get ready for your mortgage.

blocks.body: Lenders require homeowners insurance. Standard homeowners policies do not cover flood damage; flood coverage is a separate policy (NFIP or private), usually with a waiting period before it takes effect. They do not cover earthquake damage either, so read the policy's other exclusions and deductibles. Most lenders also require a lender's title policy, which protects the amount they lend; an owner's title policy is optional and protects you if someone later says they have a claim against the home from before you bought it.
blocks.plain: Lenders require homeowners insurance. A standard homeowners policy does not cover flood damage. Flood insurance is a separate policy (from NFIP or a private insurer), and there is usually a waiting period before it starts. A standard policy does not cover earthquake damage either. Read what else your policy leaves out and how much you pay first on a claim (the deductible). Most lenders also make you buy a lender's title policy, which protects the amount they lend. An owner's title policy is your choice. It protects you if someone later says they have a claim against the home from before you bought it.

blocks.body: On a conventional loan, the lender must drop PMI automatically when the balance is scheduled to reach 78% of the original value and you are current on payments, and you can request removal at 80%. Note the date. FHA mortgage insurance follows HUD's rules instead: on FHA loans started after mid-2013, the annual premium lasts the whole loan term (up to 30 years) if you borrowed more than 90% of the home's value, and up to 11 years otherwise. Your Closing Disclosure names the loan type.
blocks.plain: With a conventional loan, the lender must drop private mortgage insurance on its own once your balance is scheduled to reach 78% of the home's original value and you are up to date on payments. You can ask for it to be removed at 80%. Write down the date. FHA loans follow HUD's rules instead. On FHA loans started after mid-2013, if you borrowed more than 90% of the home's value, the yearly premium lasts for the whole loan (up to 30 years). If you borrowed 90% or less, it lasts up to 11 years. Your Closing Disclosure shows which loan type you have.
props: PMI terminates automatically at scheduled 78% of original value (conventional loans)
Automatic termination happens once you are current on payments
FHA mortgage insurance follows HUD's rules, not these

Checker 2026-11-16: 'if you are current' became 'and you are current', because 12 U.S.C. 4902(b)(2) still ends PMI once a late borrower becomes current (the 'if' read as a condition that could forfeit removal); '(up to 30 years)' added because HUD says 'end of the loan term, or 30 years, whichever occurs first'. 'Started after mid-2013' stands for 'FHA case numbers assigned on or after June 3, 2013'; older FHA loans follow other rules. CFP-27's 'refinancing is the usual way out' is not included: not read at a primary source. 'Lender' is kept from the current text, though the statute and CFPB say the servicer does this; the owner may want 'servicer'. Borrower-requested cancellation at 80% also has conditions (written request, good payment history, possibly proof of value; 12 U.S.C. 4902(a)) that the current text does not name; no finding raised it. Numbers set: {78%, 80%, 2013, 30, 90%, 11} in both variants.

blocks.body: Owning a home raises what you can lose in a lawsuit. An umbrella policy sits on top of homeowners and auto liability. While your equity and savings are still small, it may not be worth the premium yet; revisit it as your net worth grows.
blocks.plain: Owning a home raises what you could lose if someone sues you. An umbrella policy adds coverage on top of your home and auto liability. If you have little home equity or savings so far, it may not be worth the cost yet. Look at it again as your net worth grows.
props: Owning a home raises lawsuit exposure
Umbrella sits on top of homeowners and auto liability

blocks.body: Gain on selling a main home can be excluded up to {{fig:sec121_exclusion_single}} ({{fig:sec121_exclusion_mfj}} on a qualifying joint return) if you owned and lived in it for two of the five years before the sale. Capital improvements add to your basis, so keep the receipts.

Money spent on improvements raises your cost basis, so keep the receipts.

owner_decisions.what: Add a 'First year' step to the home-purchase playbook: apply for any property-tax homestead exemption by the local deadline, and confirm how the deed is titled.

draft.title: Check the property-tax exemption and how the deed is titled
draft.body: In many states the county or local tax office offers a homestead or owner-occupant property-tax exemption that you have to apply for, often by a deadline, so check with yours. Also confirm how the deed is titled, because the form of ownership affects who owns the home if one owner dies.
draft.plain: In many states, your county or local tax office gives owners who live in their home a lower property tax, but you have to apply, often by a deadline. Check with yours. Also check how your deed names the owners, because that affects who owns the home if one owner dies.
